body:
CC @mihe @jrouwe 

Tagging `bug` for now as the difference in behavior seems unexpected, but can reclassify in case it's an expected difference with how Jolt manages collisions.

Haven't looked into it but this reminds me of old issues with Godot Physics where physics colliders would first be instantiated at the scene origin before being moved to their expected location, generating a ton of unexpected collisions at load time. Maybe the Jolt integration does something similar.

This is a known performance discrepancy (that probably should be mentioned in [the documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/physics/using_jolt_physics.html)), which stems from the fact that compound shapes (i.e. bodies with multiple shapes) are rebuilt from scratch every time you make any modification to the compound shape when using Jolt, including when changing any of the shapes' properties, which is a fairly costly operation, especially with this many sub-shapes. I mentioned this in #99895 under the "Compound shapes" header, but it didn't end up being translated into a more user-friendly version in the documentation unfortunately.

@diegopau There is one simple workaround to this, which is to simply move your `add_child(static_body)` to the bottom of `_ready`. This exploits the fact that the underlying Jolt shapes aren't actually committed/built/created until you add a body to a physics "space" (i.e. a scene tree). So basically, you need to build up the body's entire shape before you add it as a child to another node.

#101189 was made specifically to lessen the cost of this whole problem, but it only makes a relatively small dent, unfortunately.

Me and @jrouwe have been [discussing](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/discussions/1165) other alternative approaches to this, which would significantly speed things up, but the refactoring needed to get there are scary and fairly comprehensive, so I haven't taken the time to explore it yet.

@mihe Thank you for replying here so quickly! I did test to do as you said for the MRP and move add_child(static_body) to the end of the _ready and it indeed fixes the issue completely in the MRP.

For the full game I am working on (which I can't give many details about) I tried to use this new knowledge and try to understand up to what point I could use similar solutions (preparing the collisions outside the tree, add them to the active scene once they are ready), but I think that would imply to completely change how the game is built. Let me explain:

The game is a blocky game, so think of Minecraft or Cubeworld but in this case it won't be generating chunks of blocky terrain as you move around. This is using pre-made Godot scenes that are just loaded and unloaded as you move from one area of the game to the next, though it sometimes loads several areas at once (it's a blocky game but not an open world game, so this sort of strategy works well here).
Now, each of the scenes (areas of the game) has a mix of:
- Gridmaps, each gridmaps having many meshes and each mesh being a block with its box3D collision shape. Gridmaps are convenient for blocks that should be possible to destroy independently.
- Big meshinstance3D objects, that represents blocky terrain that does not need to be destroyed block by block. So the blocky terrain is done with an external software and an .obj is imported to Godot. For this what I do is to generate all the needed collisions with a script (in this case is not one per block since blocks are not independent, but due to the nature of the blocky mesh, still hundreds or even thousands of collisions are needed to cover the whole detail of the terrain) those collisions are added to a StaticBody3D, saved as a separate scene and added to the main scene of the level. So the collisions are not added in runtime, they are all pre-generated and already added to the scene.

So the most basic scene could be something like this:
```
MyGameArea
    GridMapDestructibleBlocks
    MeshInstance3DTerrain
    TerrainCollisionsForTheMesh
```
and in case you are curious, i don't do the whole thing with gridmaps (which would be even better since I don't have to mix two systems and i would have all blocks fully independent without further tricks), because there is a limit to how many GridMap cells Godot is able to handle without giving issues (seems to be at around 4 million) and I would then have to do more complex stuff like loading chunks and so on.

So basically you end up having a mix of gridmaps and meshes with their collisions all loaded up together with the scene. So maybe the recommended way for Jolt usage would be to not have those gridmaps and terrain collisions added to the scene and tell the script to load them separately and them add them to the scene? but that implies that our scenes would not be built in the same way ready to preview, and maybe other things that happen during the _ready function of the scenes that assume that those other nodes are already there.

I am still kind of new to Godot so maybe there is another workaround for this.

In any case, if this is part of how Jolt works (for now, unless you work on that other approach) I do think it would be helpful to document it clearly so people don't see it as a bug. Maybe the currently default physics will keep being the best option for a very small percentage of games (like this one) and that is fine, luckily for me the game I am working on is kind of simple in terms of physics so I might not really need any of the improvements that Jolt offers.

> The game is a blocky game, so think of Minecraft or Cubeworld but in this case it won't be generating chunks of blocky terrain as you move around.

For what it's worth, this issue is prominently visible in Godot's own [Voxel Game Demo](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/2755) as well, which does chunked streaming as you move around, and which adds the shapes after the body has been added to the scene tree. However, with some minor changes that can be made to work well-ish enough with Jolt as-is.

> So the most basic scene could be something like this:
> 
> ```
> MyGameArea
>     GridMapDestructibleBlocks
>     MeshInstance3DTerrain
>     TerrainCollisionsForTheMesh
> ```

Which of these is causing the problem? None of these should inherently be a problem, as far as I know, and mixing them like this shouldn't be an issue either. Having many collision shapes isn't a problem per se, only the act of adding the shapes to the body after the body's been added to the scene tree is, and ready-made scenes with tons of shapes in it isn't a problem, since they get childed before its parent (the body) is added to the scene tree.

> In any case, if this is part of how Jolt works (for now, unless you work on that other approach) I do think it would be helpful to document it clearly so people don't see it as a bug.

Yes, I'll see about adding some explanation (and the workaround) to the documentation for now, but just to be clear, this can and will be fixed properly at some point.

> Which of these is causing the problem? None of these should inherently be a problem, as far as I know, and mixing them like this shouldn't be an issue either. Having many collision shapes isn't a problem per se, only the act of adding the shapes to the body after the body's been added to the scene tree is, and ready-made scenes with tons of shapes in it isn't a problem, since they get childed before its parent (the body) is added to the scene tree.

You are right. I was in the mindset that the problem was having the StaticBody3D with the collisions already in the scene when running the game (as opposed to loading the StaticBody3D outside of the active scene and then add it to the scene). But now that you reminded me that the issue is about adding the shapes to the body when the body is already in the scene... I don't really know what is going on. Please let me review the project I am working on and try to isolate what exactly causes the issue. Might take me a day or two since I don't have a lot of time for that project this week but I should be able to come up with an explanation or another MRP isolating the issue.

I can confirm this on 4.5.dev 215acd52e while editing the 3D platformer demo level. Switching to GodotPhysics3D avoids the performance issue. You can mitigate this by reducing octant size in GridMap (I've had good results with values between 6 and 10 instead of the default 16).

@mihe What I found out is already confirmed by you and @Calinou but I thought I should still explain my findings and attach the new MRP in case it is useful.

What was creating the big difference in the game I am working on are the gridmap nodes, not the other nodes that contain thousands of collisions for the meshes imported from .obj.
The game starts, loads the current area and also adjacent areas. The loading itself seems to happen very fast, but its the process of adding the areas (scenes containing gridmaps with thousands of cells) to the active scene what seems to block for Godot for a while... actually it seems to happen after they are added but in some sort of parallel process that I can't control through my code. I say this because I print stuff to screen after doing active_scene.add_child(level_area) and those get printed very fast but it gets stuck later on when apparently nothing is being done by my code, so i believe is when Godot is trying to actually render what has been added to the active scene.

In any case it is more clear in this MRP I think.

Please unzip and open the project and check that at this moment Jolt physics are enabled. Do not run the whole project, instead please open the folder "scene6" and open the scene "scene6_built_by_adding_other_GRIDMAP_scenes_on_runtime.tscn", then just run that scene. 

In my computer it takes around 45 seconds to load the scene. This is a scene that instantiates and adds to the scene a total of 18 subscenes each containing a gridmap with 15000 cells so we have a total of 270000 cells. This is important because initially i was doing tests with 45000 cells and i couldn't really see any issues, but then i realize that the game I am working on is having around 150000 cells loaded so I then I tried increasing the number to something similar in the MRP scene and it shows that more than the loading time increasing linearly it is more like an exponential problem or maybe a threshold.

If you open Godot with the console you will see that the console already prints print("Instances are now added") which is the very last thing the script does, and is after that that Godot is stuck for a while

If you now switch to Godot default physics engine, then the load is instant in my computer, less than a second.

In the MRP there are other scenes and things that might be useful, like in that scene6 you can use the number keys 1-9 of your keyboard to switch off/on processing for each of the instances loaded, and key 0 to turn them all on/off. And you have a scene5 that has a similar setup but with meshes and collisions (instead of gridmaps) and that one loads very fast.

[collisions jolt MRP-4_4_1.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19867239/collisions.jolt.MRP-4_4_1.zip)

I have run into this shape rebuild problem in my rope library:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/117737

I also experienced an issue with the performance of changing collision shapes (or, actually, just adding collision shapes) to a physics body via `GridMap`

My game is procedurally generating relatively small levels, but the blocks are pretty big, and each contain 8-12 basic collision shapes (all `BoxShape3D`'s). In `GridMap`, each octant has a physics body, and the shapes for each block get added to their octant's body. As best as I can tell, each subsequent shape added to the octant seems to take longer and longer to add?

Anyway, even though my levels are pretty small, it was taking something like 30 seconds for generation to finish. However, if I change the Octant Size on the `GridMap` from 8 (the default) to 4, it takes less than a second (which is what I'm currently using in my game as a workaround). I think this is because each octant gets much fewer collision shapes added to it, and since it seems like each additional shape takes longer and longer to add, the difference in wall time is pretty big.

There's a number of workarounds, of course! There's changing the Octant Size (like I did), but I could also have switched from a bunch of `BoxShape3D`s to a polygon shape (although, this could have made collision slower?), or removing the `GridMap` from the tree when doing the procedural generation
